newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: Shrinking Aral Sea is killing Uzbek town.
newsitem.headline: Shrinking Aral Sea is killing Uzbek town.

text.p: Once a green, bustling seaport, Muynak is dying slowly in a salty desert, its fate tied inextricably to the shrinking Aral Sea.
Lying about 1,000 km (600 miles) west of the Uzbek capital Tashkent, the town of 14,000 is one of the worst hit by the receding waters in what was once the world's fourth largest lake.

On Friday the leaders of the five former Soviet republics of Central Asia -- Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan -- meet in the Kazakh capital Almaty to discuss the plight of the inland sea.

The saga of one of the region's worst ecological disasters dates back to the 1960s when the then Soviet leadership decided to boost cotton production in its central Asian colonies and ordered vast amounts of water drawn from the mighty Syr Darya and Amu Darya rivers to irrigate the crops. The rivers feed the Aral.

Four decades ago, about 60 cubic km of fresh water flowed into the sea every year. Now only one to five cubic km trickles through annually, depending on rainfall. At least 35 cubic km are generally considered the minimum to halt the shoreline shrinkage.

In Muynak, a steamboat perches forlornly on a pedestal, a monument to times past, and faded, Soviet-era posters depict cheerful fishermen, nets groaning with fish, on boards in front of the town's administrative building.
Just a few hundred metres (yards) away, hulks of old ships and piles of anchor chains lie rusting in a sea of sand shifting in the wind at what used to be the quayside.
The old embankment gives way to grey sand and scrub where the blue waters of the Aral once washed the shore. The Aral now is 120 km (80 miles) north of Muynak.
The town museum exhibits flowers, wildfowl, otters and other fauna that once flourished around Muynak but which have now disappeared.
"We had all these," said Muratbay, the elderly museum keeper, pointing at the vanished species housed in glass jars. "But now we have nothing, only salt."
Despair reigns in Muynak.
"Cotton is drinking our sea," said Sali Kulimov, a retired doctor. "There is no way to live."
Many houses in the town are shells and the fish cannery, the only enterprise left, struggles to stay open, relying on fish shipped in from the Caspian Sea and the distant waters of the Baltic.
Local officials were reluctant to comment on Uzbekistan's strongman president, Islam Karimov's plan to boost this year's raw cotton harvest to four million tonnes, from 3.35 million tonnes in 1996.
But the head of the Muynak district, Uytimurat Kalmuratov, said: "The ecological catastrophe of the Aral Sea outweighs the advantages of higher cotton production."

About 3.5 million people live in the disaster-hit area and health officials in Nukus, capital of the republic's western Karakalpak autonomous region, told Reuters they had detected a sharp growth in diseases, many of them fatal.
They said over one third of the population suffered from anaemia, adding that the figure rose to 72 percent among the region's expectant mothers.
The number of anaemia-sufferers has soared 600 times to 3,716 for every 10,000 people in 1996, from just six per 10,000 in 1980.
Along with high rates of kidney diseases, every ninth inhabitant in Muynak suffers from tuberculosis.
Streets and houses in Muynak are covered with a thick layer of fine sand and salt blown off the dry sea bed, containing poisonous chemicals washed off the heavily fertilised cotton fields.
Doctors say the ubiquitous dust, which gets inside clothes and is inhaled, is the town's number one killer.

Nurlybek Mirzamuratov, a representative of Uzbekistan's ecological movement Ecosan and an ethnic Karakalpak, said Russians and Kazakhs were able to leave for their own states. "We Karakalpaks settled on the Aral centuries ago but now we have nowhere to go," he said.
